People assume we exist to keep sport out of the courts, and that is not quite it. The reason is speed and the reason is uniformity. A player is transferred in July and the window shuts in September. A judge in one country will take three years to decide what a clause means, and by then the season it mattered in is history. So the parties agree in advance to come to us, and they agree that what we hand down is final. It is often said that the athlete has no real choice about that, and in practice the athlete does not. What I would say is that the choice was never between this tribunal and a perfect trial. It was between this tribunal and twenty-eight national answers to the same question, which is how you end up with a rule that means one thing in Madrid and another in Manchester.

The public picture of match-fixing is a brown envelope in a car park, and in eleven years I have never seen one. What we see is betting data. A market that moves at three in the morning, in a country with no interest in the match, on an outcome nobody would price that way, and it moves before anything at all has happened on the pitch. That is the alert. Then the slow part starts, and the slow part is where most files die, because the money is believed to have moved through four jurisdictions and we can compel disclosure in none of them. People are often reported to have been charged when what has actually happened is that they have been provisionally suspended while we ask questions. The difference matters enormously to them, and it is never in the headline.

An alert is raised, usually by data rather than by a person, and the governing body opens a file. The athlete is notified and, under most codes, provisionally suspended while the file is built. A hearing is held, on paper or in a room, and both sides put their case. A first-instance panel hands down a decision, and either a sanction is imposed or the athlete is cleared. And then, within twenty-one days, either side may take the whole thing to arbitration in Lausanne, where a final award is made and no ordinary court will reopen it.
